prompt: A GitOps application is OutOfSync after an emergency live patch. Decide whether to self-heal and restore a safe source of truth.
directAnswer: Bind cluster/application/source/destination, resolved commit and render digest, live object UID, tracking metadata, managed fields, audit actor/change ticket, emergency intent and expiry, plus the user SLI. OutOfSync proves difference only. If the patch is an authorized mitigation, immediate self-heal may reintroduce the incident; time-bound reconciliation suspension or a narrowly scoped ignore can be justified by the incident commander. Encode the required state in the authoritative repository through reviewed change, remove the temporary exception, reconcile the exact revision, verify rollout and user recovery, and retain the audit timeline. If the patch is unauthorized, contain access and reconcile only after ensuring desired state is safe.
foundation: Drift needs ownership and intent classification before correction.
reasoningSteps: Tie audit actor to change authority.
Check user impact and source safety.
seniorAnswer: I do not let a self-healing controller erase a valid emergency mitigation before source catches up; I also refuse to let break-glass become a second permanent source of truth.
weakAnswer: Git is truth, so enable self-heal and overwrite the patch.
whyWeak: The desired revision may be the cause of the active incident and automated correction can restore harm.

evidence.proves: who changed the field and under what recorded intent

evidence.signal: reviewed commit, reconcile and user SLI

followUps.prompt: Why not keep the live patch?
followUps.answer: It is unauditable desired-state divergence and continuous reconciliation may erase it later.

followUps.prompt: When is an ignore rule safe?
followUps.answer: Only for exact fields owned by a known controller, with tests proving it cannot hide security or availability drift.
Named owner, deadline, follow-up source change and alert when suspension/divergence remains.
